title: Handover, reports and structured communication
blurb: Use SBAR, give clear handovers and delegation instructions, and share digital information safely.
question: Nurse Femi phones the on-call doctor about Mrs Grant, 79, whose NEWS2 has risen to 6. He says, "I think she may be developing sepsis." Which part of SBAR is he giving?

teach.body: Information lost or muddled at handover is a classic cause of harm. The NMC proficiencies ask you to present verbal and written reports confidently (Annexe A 1.9), give clear verbal, digital or written instructions when delegating or handing over (1.11) and record and share digital information safely (1.10). In plain English: say the right things, in a predictable order, to the right person, and make sure it was understood.
teach.cite: NMC Standards of proficiency (2018) Annexe A 1.9-1.11; Code 8.2, 8.3

letters.word: Situation: who, where, what's happening now
Assessment: what you think the problem is
Recommendation: what you need, by when

teach.h: Scenario: Nurse Femi calls the doctor
teach.body: S: "I'm Femi, staff nurse on Ward 7. I'm calling about Mrs Grant in bed 4: her NEWS2 has risen from 2 to 6." B: "She's 79, admitted two days ago with a urinary infection, and has type 2 diabetes." A: "Her respiratory rate is 24 and she's newly confused. I think she may be developing sepsis." R: "I need you to review her within 30 minutes. Can you confirm when you'll arrive?"

head: Statement
Element
rows: "She has COPD and had surgery on Monday"
"Please review her in the next 30 minutes"

teach.h: Recommendation means a clear, timed request
teach.body: A vague call ("just letting you know") invites a vague response. Say exactly what you need and when, and agree it. If the response does not match the urgency, escalate: Code 16.1 asks you to raise and, if necessary, escalate concerns. With NEWS2 of 7 or more the RCP standard is an emergency assessment by a team with critical care competencies, so waiting two hours for a junior doctor is not acceptable.

teach.h: Handover that helps versus handover that harms
teach.caption: Code 10.2: identify risks and the steps taken so colleagues have the information they need. Code 10.4: no unnecessary abbreviations or jargon.

teach.h: Delegating or handing over a task clearly
items: Delegate only to someone competent to do the task (Code 11.1).
Give specific instructions: what, when, and the exact findings to report back.
Supervise and confirm the outcome meets the required standard (Code 11.3).
Remember: you stay accountable for the decision to delegate.

teach.h: Taking a critical result by phone

steps.label: Record
steps.sub: Who you told, when, and the plan

teach.body: Send personal information through approved, secure systems, share the minimum necessary for the purpose (Caldicott principle 3), and access records only on a need-to-know basis (principle 4). UK GDPR requires integrity and confidentiality (security). Personal email, messaging apps and photos on a personal phone are not approved routes. The duty to share for individual care is as important as the duty to protect confidentiality (principle 7).
teach.cite: Code 10.5; Caldicott principles (2020); UK GDPR Art 5

teach.text: Background is not Assessment. Age, diagnosis and history are Background; YOUR interpretation ("I think she's septic") is Assessment. And a Recommendation is a request with a time frame, not a summary.

items: SBAR: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation (NHS England, 2017).
Handover names risks, timings, trends and what's been done (Code 10.2, 8.3).
Delegation: competent person, specific instructions, check understanding, supervise, confirm outcome (Code 11).
Critical results by phone: write, read back, act, record.
Digital sharing: approved secure systems, minimum necessary, need to know (Caldicott, UK GDPR).

summary: You can now structure a call or handover with SBAR, identify each element, give delegation instructions that are specific and checked, and escalate when the response does not match the urgency. You also know how to share digital information safely.

A.q: Using SBAR, Nurse Mai tells the doctor, "She is 74, had a bowel resection two days ago and has COPD." Which SBAR element is this?
options: Situation
Assessment
Background
Recommendation
A.why: Background gives relevant history and context such as age, admission reason and past medical history (NHS England SBAR guide, 2017).

whyNot.0: Situation is the immediate problem that prompted the call.
whyNot.1: Assessment is the nurse's interpretation of what the problem is.
whyNot.3: Recommendation is the specific request, such as a review within a set time.

A.q: Nurse Ali tells the doctor, "His urine output has fallen and his mouth is dry. I think he's becoming dehydrated." Which SBAR element is the final sentence?
options: Assessment
Recommendation
Situation
Background
A.why: Assessment is the nurse's interpretation of what the problem is (NHS England SBAR guide, 2017). It sounds like a fact, but it is his clinical judgement.

whyNot.1: A Recommendation is a specific request with a time frame, such as a review within 30 minutes.
whyNot.2: Situation is the immediate problem stated at the start of the call.
whyNot.3: Background is the relevant history and context, such as age and admission reason.

A.q: At the end of a shift, which item is most important for Nurse Ben to include when handing over Mrs Webb, 77?
options: Her daughter is visiting at about seven o'clock this evening
Her IV antibiotic is due at 18:00 and her NEWS2 has risen to 4
She prefers tea with milk and likes the radio on in the morning
She was admitted through the emergency department late on Tuesday
A.why: Handover should name risks, timings and trends so colleagues can act (Annexe A 1.11; Code 10.2, 8.3). A rising NEWS2 and a time-critical medicine are the priorities.

whyNot.0: Visiting times are useful but not safety-critical.
whyNot.2: Preferences matter for person-centred care but are lower priority than a rising NEWS2.
whyNot.3: Route of admission is background that does not need action this shift.

B.q: Nurse Rose delegates afternoon observations on Mrs Lee, 81, to a healthcare assistant. Which instruction is clearest?
options: "Can you keep an eye on Mrs Lee this afternoon and let me know how she is?"
"Please do Mrs Lee's obs when you get a moment this afternoon."
"Check Mrs Lee is okay after lunch; she was a bit pale earlier."
"Do her obs at 14:00 and tell me at once if systolic is below 100."
B.why: Code 11.1-11.2: delegate within competence and make sure instructions are fully understood. A clear time and an explicit reporting threshold make the task safe (Annexe A 1.11).

whyNot.0: 'Keep an eye on' does not say what to check or what to report.
whyNot.1: No set time or reporting threshold is given.
whyNot.2: 'Check she is okay' is vague and gives no measurable trigger for reporting.

B.q: A laboratory scientist phones the ward with a potassium of 6.8 mmol/L for Mr Shaw. What is the most appropriate way for the nurse to take this result?
options: Write it down, read it back, then tell the doctor at once
Note it on a scrap of paper and add it to the handover sheet
Ask the laboratory to email the result to the doctor instead
Remember the value and tell the doctor on the evening round
B.why: Recording and reading back confirms accuracy, and a critical result needs timely referral (Code 13.2) and an accurate record (Code 10.1).

whyNot.1: A scrap of paper is not a secure record and handover delays action.
whyNot.2: Diverting the result delays action on a potentially dangerous value.
whyNot.3: Relying on memory risks error, and waiting for a round delays treatment.

B.q: A practice nurse needs to send a patient's wound photographs and care plan to the community nursing team. Which method is most appropriate?
options: Email them from her personal account marked 'confidential'
Send them through the approved, secure NHS system
Text the photos from her phone to the district nurse
Print them and leave them at reception for collection
B.why: Annexe A 1.10: share digital information safely. Code 10.5 keep records secure; UK GDPR integrity and confidentiality require approved, secure routes.

whyNot.0: A personal account is not an approved or secure route, whatever the subject line says.
whyNot.2: Patient images on a personal phone are not secure and breach data protection.
whyNot.3: Unattended printouts at reception risk unauthorised access.

C.q: Mr Long's NEWS2 is 7. The nurse calls the junior doctor using SBAR, who says he will come "when he can", in about two hours. What should the nurse do next?
options: Wait for the doctor and repeat the observations every hour
Record the call and hand the concern over to the night team
Escalate now to a senior doctor or critical care outreach
Call the doctor back in an hour if the score has gone higher
C.why: NEWS2 7 or more requires an emergency assessment by a team with critical care competencies and continuous monitoring (RCP 2017). Code 16.1: escalate concerns if the response is not adequate.

whyNot.0: A score of 7 needs continuous monitoring and an emergency response, not hourly observations and a wait.
whyNot.1: Handing over delays escalation of a patient at high risk.
whyNot.3: Waiting an hour for further deterioration is unsafe at this score.

C.q: Nurse Imani is handing over a patient at the bedside. The patient, who has capacity, is awake. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Lower her voice so the patient will not be worried by the details
Invite the patient to add to the handover and check their views
Hand over at the station first, then introduce the new nurse
Use abbreviations so the handover is quicker and more discreet
C.why: Involving the person reflects partnership (Code 2.1, 2.3) and allows them to correct or add information, making the handover safer.

whyNot.0: Talking about a person with capacity in front of them while excluding them is not partnership.
whyNot.2: This can be appropriate for sensitive detail, but the patient is awake and able to contribute now.
whyNot.3: Code 10.4 discourages unnecessary abbreviations and jargon, which increase misunderstanding.

C.q: Nurse Owen asks a healthcare assistant to help Mrs Kaur, 88, to walk to the bathroom. The assistant has not used the frame Mrs Kaur needs. What should Owen do?
options: Ask the assistant to try it and call for help if she struggles
Show the assistant how to use the frame and supervise this time
Leave a note on the frame describing how to adjust it correctly
Tell Mrs Kaur to use a commode until a physiotherapist visits
C.why: Code 11.1: delegate only within the other person's competence; Code 11.2-11.3: make sure they understand, supervise and confirm the outcome.

whyNot.0: Delegating a task the assistant is not competent in risks a fall.
whyNot.2: A note does not confirm competence or understanding.
whyNot.3: This restricts Mrs Kaur unnecessarily when the assistant can be shown and supervised.

reteach.title: Tell the story in the order the listener needs it
reteach.question: If the person on the phone could only remember four things, what would you want them to be?

blocks.body: SBAR runs in the order a busy colleague needs: what is happening NOW (Situation), what led here THEN (Background), SO what you think it means (Assessment), and PLEASE do this by this time (Recommendation). If you can't say your Recommendation, decide what you want before you pick up the phone.

blocks.text: "I think he's dehydrated" is Assessment, even though it sounds like a fact. Your interpretation always sits in A.

explain.body: Situation: who you are, where you are, who the patient is and what's happening now. Background: the relevant history (age, admission reason, past history, recent treatment).

test.q: "I'm calling about Mr Ito in bed 9: his oxygen saturation has dropped to 89% on air." Which SBAR element is this?
options: Background
Assessment
Recommendation
Situation
test.why: This states who and what is happening now: the Situation.

explain.body: Assessment is your clinical judgement about the problem. Recommendation is a clear, timed request. If the response doesn't match the urgency, escalate (Code 16.1).

test.q: Which statement is the best example of an SBAR Recommendation?
options: "I think he may have a chest infection."
"Please review him within 30 minutes."
"He's had a productive cough since Monday."
"His temperature is now 38.6 degrees."
test.why: A Recommendation is a specific request with a time frame.

whyNot.3: This is part of the Situation or Assessment findings.

explain.body: Delegate within competence (Code 11.1), give specific instructions with what to report and when, check understanding, supervise, and confirm the outcome (11.2-11.3). You remain accountable for the decision to delegate.

test.q: When a registered nurse delegates a task to a healthcare assistant, who is accountable for the decision to delegate?
options: The healthcare assistant
The ward manager on duty
The registered nurse
The patient's consultant
test.why: Code 11: you are accountable for your decision to delegate; the person accepting is accountable for carrying out the task.

whyNot.0: The assistant is accountable for how they carry out the task, not the decision to delegate it.
whyNot.1: The manager is not accountable for an individual nurse's delegation decision.
whyNot.3: The consultant did not make the delegation decision.

explain.body: Use approved secure systems, share the minimum necessary, access records only when you need to for care, and keep records secure (Code 10.5; Caldicott 3, 4; UK GDPR integrity and confidentiality).

test.q: A nurse is referring a patient to a dietitian electronically. How much of the record should she share?
options: The full record so the dietitian has context
The information relevant to the referral
Her own summary without the diagnosis
Whatever the patient's family has agreed to
test.why: Caldicott principle 3: use the minimum necessary personal confidential data; UK GDPR data minimisation.

whyNot.0: Sharing the whole record exceeds what is necessary.
whyNot.2: The diagnosis may be relevant to nutrition and leaving it out could harm care.
whyNot.3: Family agreement does not determine what is shared for an adult's care.
